questions.question: The Eagle effect.
questions.question_raw: Eagle Effect

parts.text: Describe it ("more drug kills less").
What class of antibiotic is affected?

parts_raw.text: A. Describe it. ("more drug kill less")
B. What class of antibiotic is affected?

questions.model_answer:
a) The Eagle effect is the paradoxical observation that killing of a large, dense, or stationary-phase inoculum is reduced at very high antibiotic concentrations compared with lower concentrations. Because killing by these agents requires active cell-wall synthesis, organisms in stationary phase (few actively dividing cells, low PBP turnover) are killed less efficiently, and escalating the dose does not improve, and may worsen, in-vitro killing.
b) β-Lactams (classically penicillin), the cell-wall-active agents whose killing depends on actively growing/dividing bacteria.
questions.beyond_mandell: Eagle effect is not described in this chapter slice; answer rests on established pharmacology (Eagle's original penicillin/streptococcal work).

cohort_answer.text: Paradoxical reduction in antimicrobial killing activity with high concentrations of the drug (for bugs in stationary phase) – have less PBPs expressed when stationary. Beta lactams

questions.question: β-Lactams.
questions.question_raw: Beta lactams.

parts.text: How do they work? (2 points)
What is the best pharmacokinetic parameter to measure them?
What is a way of maximizing effectiveness given (b)?

parts_raw.text: How do they work (4 lines allotted, 2 points)
What is the best pharmacokinetic parameter to measure them?
What’s a way of maximizing the effectiveness given (b) ?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) They bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and inhibit the transpeptidase/transglycosylase activities needed to cross-link peptidoglycan, so cell-wall synthesis fails. (2) The stable acyl-PBP complex (slow deacylation) irreversibly inactivates the enzyme, and in dividing organisms this produces autolysis and bactericidal killing.
b) The time free drug concentration remains above the MIC (fT>MIC) - the governing pharmacodynamic parameter.
c) Maximize time above MIC with prolonged/extended or continuous infusion, or more frequent dosing.
questions.beyond_mandell: T>MIC and infusion strategy are established PD principles not stated in this slice.

questions.question: For the following antibiotics, describe their (i) capacity for inducing AmpC (strong/weak), (ii) susceptibility to hydrolysis by AmpC (high/low), and (iii) whether they are recommended for invasive infection.
questions.question_raw: For the following antibiotics, describe their i) capacity for inducing AmpC (strong/weak), ii) susceptibility to hydrolysis by AmpC (high/low), iii) whether they are recommended for invasive infection.

parts.text: Ceftriaxone
Cefepime
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Ceftazidime-avibactam
Imipenem

parts_raw.text: Ceftriaxone
Cefepime
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Ceftazidime-avibactam
Imipenem

questions.model_answer: a) Ceftriaxone: (i) weak inducer; (ii) high susceptibility to AmpC hydrolysis; (iii) not recommended for invasive infection by an AmpC producer (derepressed mutants emerge on therapy). b) Cefepime: (i) weak inducer; (ii) low susceptibility (zwitterion penetrates rapidly and is less susceptible to AmpC inactivation); (iii) yes — treatment of choice for serious AmpC inducible-resistant strains. c) Piperacillin-tazobactam: (i) weak inducer; (ii) high (tazobactam does not reliably inhibit AmpC, so the penicillin is hydrolysed); (iii) not recommended for invasive AmpC infection. d) Ceftazidime-avibactam: (i) weak inducer; (ii) low (avibactam inhibits class C/AmpC, restoring activity); (iii) yes — recommended for invasive AmpC producers. e) Imipenem: (i) strong inducer; (ii) low (stable to AmpC hydrolysis); (iii) yes — recommended for invasive AmpC infection.
questions.beyond_mandell: The strong/weak induction hierarchy and the pip-tazo/imipenem entries rest on standard AmpC teaching (e.g. Tamma et al., IDSA AmpC guidance); Mandell explicitly supports only that cefepime is less susceptible to AmpC and is treatment of choice for AmpC strains, and that ceftazidime-avibactam's avibactam inhibits class C enzymes.

questions.question: A patient has Streptococcus pneumoniae community-acquired pneumonia with the following MICs: penicillin 2, erythromycin 64, clindamycin 256.
questions.question_raw: Strep pneumonia CAP with MICs as follows: Pen 2; Erythro 64; Clinda 256

parts.text: Is it safe to use penicillin? Why or why not?
What is the mechanism of penicillin resistance in pneumococcus?
What are 2 types of macrolide resistance?
What type is present here?

parts_raw.text: Is it safe to use penicillin? Why or why not?
B.  What is the mechanism of pen resistance in pneumococcus?
C. What are 2 types of macrolide resistance?
d) What type is present here?

questions.model_answer:
a) Yes, for this non-CNS infection treated parenterally. Current breakpoints define a pneumococcus as penicillin-susceptible if the MIC is <=2 ug/mL for non-CNS parenteral therapy, so an MIC of 2 is susceptible IV. (It would be intermediate/resistant by the oral non-CNS breakpoint of <=0.06 and resistant by the CNS breakpoint of <=0.06, so it could not be used orally or for meningitis.)
b) Alteration of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs): mutations in the genes encoding PBPs (notably PBP2b for low-level and PBP2x/1a for high-level resistance) reduce penicillin's binding affinity. These altered genes are acquired by transformation (e.g., from S. mitis).
c) (1) Ribosomal target methylation encoded by ermB (methylates A2058 in domain V of 23S rRNA), giving high-level resistance (>=64 ug/mL) and the MLSB phenotype. (2) Efflux encoded by mefA, giving lower-level resistance (usually <=16 ug/mL), affecting macrolides only.
d) MLSB (ermB-mediated ribosomal methylation): resistance to both the macrolide (erythromycin 64) and clindamycin (256) indicates ribosomal methylation, not an efflux pump (which would spare clindamycin).

cohort_answer.text:
IV Non-meningitic: ≤2 is susceptible --- can use; Po pen: ≤0.06 µg/mL (same breakpoints as meningitis); Meningitic: pen susceptible is ≤0.06 µg/mL, resistant is ≥0.12 µg/mL
Alteration of target enzymes (PBPs)
Efflux pumps (mef in strep pneumo, mSRA in staph aureus), resistance to macrolides, not clinda (M phenotype); Target site alteration by methylation of ribosome to prevent drug binding, resistance to both macrolides, lincosamides, streptogamins (MLSB)
Target site alteration MLSB

questions.question: Give one theoretical pharmacokinetic advantage of regimen A over regimen B.
questions.question_raw: 31. Give one theoretical advantage of regimen A over regimen B based on pharmacokinetics.

parts.text: Gram-negative acute pyelonephritis: A) gentamicin once daily vs B) gentamicin thrice daily
Pseudomonas pneumonia with elevated but still-susceptible MIC to piperacillin-tazobactam: A) piperacillin-tazobactam continuous infusion vs B) piperacillin-tazobactam in separate doses
MRSA bacteremia: A) vancomycin thrice daily vs B) vancomycin twice daily

parts_raw.text: For Gram negative acute pyelonephritis: A: Gentamicin once daily, B: Gentamicin thrice daily
b) For Pseudomonas pneumonia with increased MICs, but not resistant to PIP-TAZO: A: Pip-Tazo in a continuous infusion, B: Pip-Tazo in separate doses
c) For MRSA bacteremia: A: Vancomycin thrice daily, B: Vancomycin twice daily

questions.model_answer: a) Aminoglycoside killing is concentration-dependent: a single large daily dose maximizes peak/MIC (efficacy rises to ~90% at peak/MIC >8) and exploits the PAE, while saturable proximal-tubular uptake means once-daily dosing deposits less drug in the renal cortex, lowering/delaying nephrotoxicity. b) Piperacillin-tazobactam killing is time-dependent (T>MIC); continuous infusion keeps free drug above the (elevated) MIC for the whole interval, maximizing bacterial exposure. c) Vancomycin efficacy tracks 24-h AUC/MIC; more frequent (thrice-daily) dosing raises AUC/MIC to hit target for MRSA.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the aminoglycoside rationale is drawn from this chapter; the piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin points rest on standard beta-lactam/glycopeptide PK/PD.

cohort_answer.text: Once-daily gentamicin rationale: Aminoglycoside bactericidal activity is concentration dependent - higher peak/MIC ratio gives greater rate/extent of kill; goal is to maximize drug concentration at site of infection (optimum when exposure is ~8-10x MIC). Aminoglycosides exhibit a post-antibiotic effect (PAE, 0.5-8hrs). Saturable uptake in renal tubule cell/inner ear - once daily dosing gives lower renal cortical tissue concentration than divided/continuous dosing. Adaptive resistance (first exposure effect) - down-regulation of uptake after initial exposure; longer dosing interval preserves antibacterial activity. Decreases emergence of resistant subpopulations when peak is ≥8x MIC. Continuous Pip-Tazo infusion: maintains drug levels above MIC longer (time-dependent killing), better for bugs with minimal PAE. Vancomycin TID vs BID: killing depends on 24hr AUC/MIC; more frequent dosing gives higher AUC/MIC and better killing. NB. Vancomycin is cleared renally so actual dosing depends on weight/CrCl; goal trough >15 in severe infections.

questions.question: Ceftolozane-tazobactam in multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

parts.text: Name three resistance mechanisms that it can overcome.

parts_raw.text: Ceftolozane-tazobactam in MDR pseudomonas. Name three resistance mechanisms that it can overcome.

questions.model_answer: (1) Loss/decreased expression of the OprD outer-membrane porin (carbapenem-selective permeability defect). (2) Upregulation of RND efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM, MexXY-OprM). (3) AmpC chromosomal cephalosporinase (enhanced PBP affinity keeps it active). Ceftolozane-tazobactam has enhanced affinity for P. aeruginosa PBPs and is unaffected by porin loss or efflux upregulation, so >80% of ceftazidime- or meropenem-resistant isolates remain susceptible; it does NOT overcome metallo-β-lactamases or KPC.

cohort_answer.text: Overexpression of efflux pumps; Loss of the outer membrane porin OprD; Not affected by beta lactamases both AmpC and ESBLs; Overcomes modification of PBPs

questions.model_answer: a) Aminoglycosides kill in a concentration-dependent fashion: a single high daily dose maximizes peak/MIC (efficacy ~90% at peak/MIC >8, with less emergence of resistance) and exploits the PAE, while saturable proximal-tubular uptake lowers renal cortical accumulation and delays nephrotoxicity. b) Piperacillin-tazobactam is time-dependent (T>MIC); continuous infusion keeps free concentration above the elevated MIC throughout the interval, maximizing exposure. c) Vancomycin efficacy is driven by 24-h AUC/MIC; thrice-daily dosing raises AUC/MIC toward target for MRSA.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the gentamicin rationale is from this chapter; piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin points rest on standard beta-lactam/glycopeptide PK/PD.

cohort_answer.text: Once-daily gentamicin: Higher dose gives higher concentration and post-antibiotic effect, more efficient killing; gentamicin is concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC); PAE up to 2-6 hours in vitro, longer with higher peak; Cmax/MIC >8 correlates with less emergence of resistance; possibly lower risk of oto/nephrotoxicity. PipTazo continuous infusion: Time-dependent killing agent, greater efficacy with T>MIC; continuous infusion maintains concentrations above MIC longest, option for Pseudomonas with higher MICs. Vancomycin TID vs BID: Better area under the curve; efficacy best predicted by AUC/MIC ratio (combination of T>MIC and Peak:MIC); AUC24/MIC targets can be met with shorter interval dosing or increased dose

questions.question: What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam?

parts.text: List three mechanisms.

parts_raw.text: 22. What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

questions.model_answer: (1) AmpC cephalosporinase / ESBL production (ceftolozane is stable to these and tazobactam inhibits many ESBLs). (2) Upregulation of RND efflux systems (MexAB-OprM, MexXY-OprM). (3) Loss of the OprD porin channel. These do not appreciably affect ceftolozane-tazobactam owing to its high PBP affinity; it is NOT active against metallo-β-lactamases (VIM, IMP, NDM) or class A KPC carbapenemases.

cohort_answer.text: Not affected by ESBL or AmpC enzymes; not affected by active efflux (upregulation of MexXY, MexAB); not appreciably affected by porin channel loss of OprD (cannot overcome MBL; not active against class A KPC, contrary to ceftaz-avi)

parts.text: Mechanism of action?
What is the main pharmacodynamic parameter that affects the action of the drug?

parts_raw.text: Mechanism of action?
What's the main pharmacodynamic parameter that affects the action of the drug?
Given this, what is a way to administer the drug that would make it more effective?
What percentage of patients who say they have a penicillin allergy have a positive skin test?

questions.model_answer:
a) β-Lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and irreversibly inhibit their transpeptidase/transglycosylase activity, blocking cross-linking of the peptidoglycan cell wall; the slow deacylation of the penicillin-bound PBP amounts to irreversible enzyme inhibition, arresting cell-wall synthesis and producing bactericidal killing.
b) Time-dependent killing: the fraction of the dosing interval that free drug concentration remains above the MIC (fT>MIC).
c) Maximize time above MIC by giving more frequent doses, or by prolonged/extended or continuous infusion rather than short bolus dosing.
d) Only a minority: roughly 10% or fewer of patients reporting a penicillin allergy have a positive skin test (correspondingly, >90% test negative), and <2% of those with a reported history react when challenged.
questions.beyond_mandell: The time-above-MIC PD parameter and continuous/extended-infusion strategy are established antimicrobial pharmacodynamics, not stated in this chapter slice; the skin-test-positive percentage is standard allergy teaching (the chapter states <2% react on challenge).

questions.question: For gram-positive pathogens, name the following regarding β-lactam resistance and alternatives.
questions.question_raw: For gram positive pathogens name:

parts.text: Two mechanisms of β-lactam resistance.
Two alternative agents and their mechanism of action.

parts_raw.text: 2 mechanism of beta lactam resistance
2 alternative agent and their mechanism of action

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Production of a β-lactamase (penicillinase) that hydrolyzes the β-lactam ring, e.g. staphylococcal class A penicillinase. (2) Production of a low-affinity PBP that circumvents drug binding, e.g. PBP2a in methicillin-resistant staphylococci or PBP5 in Enterococcus faecium.
b) (1) Vancomycin - binds the terminal D-alanyl-D-alanine of peptidoglycan precursors, sterically blocking transglycosylation/transpeptidation (cell-wall synthesis). (2) Daptomycin - inserts into and depolarizes the cytoplasmic membrane in a calcium-dependent manner, causing loss of membrane potential and cell death. (Linezolid, binding 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit to inhibit protein synthesis, is an acceptable alternative.)
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter grounds the two resistance mechanisms (β-lactamase; low-affinity PBP2a/PBP5) and names vancomycin as an alternative, but the detailed mechanisms of action of vancomycin/daptomycin/linezolid are established pharmacology from other chapters.

questions.question: A patient has pneumococcal pneumonia with a penicillin MIC of 2 and high MICs for clindamycin and erythromycin.
questions.question_raw: Pneumococcal pneumonia with pen MIC of 2 and high MICs for clinda and eryth.

parts.text: What is the mechanism of penicillin resistance?
Can penicillin be used here?
What is the mechanism of macrolide resistance?
Which mechanism is in play here?

parts_raw.text: What is the mechanism of pen resistance?
Can pen be used here?
What is mechanism of macrolide resistance?
Which mechanism in play here?

questions.model_answer:
a) Alteration of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) with reduced affinity for penicillin, due to mutations in PBP genes (PBP2b for low-level, PBP2x/1a for high-level resistance) acquired by transformation.
b) Yes, if given IV for this non-CNS infection: MIC <=2 ug/mL is susceptible by the non-CNS parenteral breakpoint. It could not be used orally (oral non-CNS susceptible <=0.06) or for CNS infection.
c) Two mechanisms: ermB-encoded ribosomal methylation of 23S rRNA (high-level resistance >=64, MLSB phenotype) and mefA-encoded efflux pump (lower-level resistance <=16, macrolides only).
d) MLSB (ermB ribosomal methylation): high-level resistance to both erythromycin AND clindamycin indicates methylation rather than an efflux pump.

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin: Mechanism of resistance: altered enzyme structure (PBP) with reduced affinity for the antibiotic. Can be used if IV completely (MIC ≤2). If oral (or CNS infection), cannot use it. Macrolides and Clindamycin: Most likely mechanism is ermB (methylation of ribosome binding site). This gives high level resistance to macrolides and clindamycin (MLSB phenotype). Another mechanism of resistance is mefA (efflux pump), which is low level resistance, but this does not generally impact clindamycin

questions.question: What is the mechanism of resistance for each of the following?
questions.question_raw: What is the mechanism of resistance for the following:

parts.text: Vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus (VISA)
Fluoroquinolones in Streptococcus pneumoniae
Penicillin in Enterococcus faecium
Group A Streptococcus and erythromycin

parts_raw.text: VISA
FQ in Strep. pneumoniae
Penicillin in E. faecium

questions.model_answer: a) VISA: cell-wall changes (no enterococcal van genes) - a thickened cell wall whose excess D-Ala-D-Ala termini trap vancomycin in the outer peptidoglycan layers ('decoy'/clogging), plus increased cell-wall turnover, decreased autolytic activity, increased positive cell-wall charge, and reduced Agr function (mediated by mutations in TCSs such as GraSR, VraSR, WalKR). b) Fluoroquinolones in S. pneumoniae: stepwise target mutations in DNA gyrase (gyrA) and topoisomerase IV (parC/parE), plus efflux (PmrA). c) Penicillin/ampicillin in E. faecium: low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP5 - overexpression and/or mutation reducing beta-lactam binding. d) GAS + erythromycin: (1) erm-mediated ribosomal target methylation (23S rRNA) giving the MLSB phenotype and (2) mef-mediated macrolide efflux pump.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the VISA mechanism is in the slice (pp. 378-379); the S. pneumoniae fluoroquinolone, E. faecium PBP5, and GAS erm/mef mechanisms are from established Mandell/antimicrobial resistance knowledge (other chapters).

cohort_answer.text: VISA: Increased cell wall turnover. Increased thickness of cell wall and cross linking of peptidoglycan. S. pneumo with moxifloxacin - DNA gyrase, Topoisomerase IV. GAS with erythromycin - Erm gene - methylation of target site (MLSB phenotype); mef gene - efflux pump. E. faecium w/ penicillin: altered PBP5 - Overexpression

questions.model_answer: a) Once-daily gentamicin: maximizes peak/MIC (concentration-dependent kill, less resistance at peak/MIC >8), exploits the PAE, and reduces renal cortical accumulation via saturable uptake, lowering/delaying nephrotoxicity; also simpler and cheaper. b) Thrice-daily gentamicin: needed for synergy dosing in enterococcal endocarditis, and allows peak/trough monitoring where PK is unpredictable (burns, pregnancy, altered volume of distribution). c) Continuous piperacillin-tazobactam: time-dependent killing, so extended infusion maximizes T>MIC, useful for organisms with elevated MICs. d) Intermittent (QID) piperacillin-tazobactam: convenience/practicality of administration. e) Thrice-daily vancomycin: raises 24-h AUC/MIC toward target for maximal killing. f) Twice-daily vancomycin: convenience, adherence, and potentially less toxicity.
questions.beyond_mandell: Aminoglycoside points are from this chapter; piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin points rest on standard PK/PD teaching.

cohort_answer.text: Once daily gentamicin: convenience/adherence, less renal toxicity risk (saturable proximal tubule accumulation), concentration-dependent killing, post-antibiotic effect. TID gentamicin: can monitor trough/peak levels for PK adjustment (burns, pregnancy, renal impairment), better for synergy in endocarditis. Pip-tazo continuous infusion: time-dependent killing supports extended-infusion dosing, increasing time over MIC. Pip-tazo QID: convenience of dosing. Vancomycin TID: killing depends on AUC/MIC, allows higher AUC/MIC for maximum bactericidal effect. Vancomycin BID: convenience, adherence, less toxicity risk

questions.model_answer: a) Beta-lactamase-producing oral anaerobic gram-negative rods: (1) pigmented Prevotella spp. (2) Fusobacterium spp. (Porphyromonas spp. also acceptable). b) Aerobes/facultatives, which lie outside metronidazole's spectrum: (1) viridans streptococci (2) Actinomyces spp. c) Metronidazole must be reductively activated by low-redox electron carriers (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase/ferredoxin) found only in anaerobes; the reduced nitro radical breaks bacterial DNA strands. Aerobes lack these carriers and oxygen re-oxidizes the intermediate, so the drug is never activated.
questions.beyond_mandell: Reductive-activation mechanism is standard pharmacology, not given in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Bugs not covered by amox: Fusobacterium (some resistance to PCN, significant resistance to clindamycin and linezolid; susceptible to Flagyl, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos and carbapenems); Prevotella (significant resistance to clindamycin; susceptible to Flagyl, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos, carbapenems, linezolid); Porphyromonas (susceptible to Flagyl and beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos, carbapenems, linezolid; significant resistance to clindamycin); Peptostreptococcus. Bugs not covered by metronidazole: all the aerobes - Streptococcus, Moraxella, Lactobacillus, Enterobacteriaceae. Why metronidazole only covers anaerobes: the enzyme that activates/oxidizes metronidazole (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase / ferredoxin) is only present in anaerobic bacteria, not aerobic ones.

questions.model_answer:
a) They bind PBPs and inhibit the transpeptidase-mediated cross-linking of peptidoglycan; the slowly reversible acyl-enzyme complex irreversibly inhibits the PBP, halting cell-wall synthesis and killing the organism.
b) Time-dependent killing - the percentage of the dosing interval that free drug stays above the MIC (fT>MIC).
c) Prolonged, extended, or continuous infusion (and/or more frequent dosing) to maximize time above MIC.
d) More than 90% will have a negative skin test (the great majority of reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed).
questions.beyond_mandell: T>MIC and continuous/extended infusion are established PD principles not in this slice; the >90% negative-skin-test figure is standard penicillin-allergy teaching.

questions.question: Name two pharmacodynamic mechanisms that explain bacterial killing and differentiate antibacterial classes, giving two example antibiotics for each.

parts.text: Name two pharmacodynamic mechanisms which explain bacterial killing and differentiate between antibacterial classes, and give two examples of antibiotics for each pharmacodynamic mechanism.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 pharmacodynamic mechanisms which explain bacterial killing and differentiate between antibacterial classes? Give two examples of antibiotics for each pharmacodynamic mechanism.

questions.model_answer: (1) Concentration-dependent killing: rate and extent of killing rise with the peak concentration (high peak/MIC or AUC/MIC), often with a prolonged post-antibiotic effect allowing extended dosing intervals - e.g. aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones (daptomycin also qualifies). (2) Time-dependent killing: efficacy depends on maintaining free drug above the MIC for a sufficient fraction of the dosing interval (fT>MIC), with little benefit from higher peaks - e.g. β-lactams (penicillins) and clindamycin/macrolides; optimized by prolonged or continuous infusion.
questions.beyond_mandell: These PD killing classifications are established antimicrobial pharmacodynamics, not covered in this chapter slice.

cohort_answer.text: Concentration-Dependent Killing: Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, Daptomycin - rate/extent of killing increases with peak drug concentration; AG and FQ also have post-antibiotic effect; can be given at longer dosing intervals than predicted by half-life. Time-Dependent Killing: all beta-lactams, Clindamycin, Macrolides - free concentration maintained above MIC for a drug-specific fraction of time between doses achieves efficacy; maximizing duration of exposure (continuous infusions) leads to greater efficacy. (Alternate answer - bacteriostatic vs bactericidal: Bacteriostatic - inhibit growth/division - Tetracycline, Linezolid, Macrolides, Clindamycin. Bactericidal - kills bacteria - all beta-lactams, TMP/SMX (sometimes), Glycopeptides (weakly), Fluoroquinolones, Aminoglycosides.)

questions.model_answer:
a) Caspofungin over fluconazole - azoles inhibit CYP3A4 and interact with carbamazepine (altered levels/toxicity), whereas the echinocandin has minimal CYP interaction.
b) Atovaquone over dapsone - dapsone causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
c) Doxycycline over clindamycin - clindamycin is strongly associated with C. difficile, while doxycycline is neither a C. difficile therapy nor a notable inducer of it. (Metronidazole is a C. difficile treatment, so it does not fit "not used for treatment.")
d) Levofloxacin over moxifloxacin - levofloxacin is renally excreted with high urinary concentrations, whereas moxifloxacin achieves poor urinary levels.
e) Valganciclovir over acyclovir - ganciclovir/valganciclovir is active against CMV; acyclovir is not reliably.
f) Ceftriaxone over cefuroxime - ceftriaxone reliably penetrates the CNS and is a standard meningitis agent, whereas cefuroxime has been associated with delayed CSF sterilization/meningitis failures.

questions.model_answer: a) Pathogen-specific: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the predominant pathogen, and rising penicillin MICs (drug-resistant S. pneumoniae, favoured by prior antibiotic use/long-term care) mean higher amoxicillin doses are needed to overcome reduced-susceptibility strains; high-dose amoxicillin is the recommended oral beta-lactam where DRSP risk applies. b) Mechanistic: beta-lactams are time-dependent killers, so efficacy depends on the free drug level exceeding the MIC for ~40-50% of the dosing interval; raising the dose increases the time above MIC and optimizes pharmacodynamic target attainment against higher-MIC pneumococci.

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanisms of resistance: state the resistance mechanism and suggested treatment for each of macrolides (and explain the D test), beta-lactamases, and Pseudomonas with carbapenems.
questions.question_raw: Q53 (2007). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Name the resistance mechanism for each, as well as suggested treatment: Macrolides (+ explain D test); Beta-lactamases; Pseudomonas and carbapenems

parts.text: State the mechanisms and treatments for each category (macrolides with the D test, beta-lactamases, and Pseudomonas with carbapenems).

parts_raw.text: State mechanisms and treatments for each category

questions.model_answer: a) Macrolides: (mechanisms) efflux via mef genes (low-level, MIC <=16) and ribosomal methylation via erm genes (high-level, MIC >=64). D test: an erythromycin disk placed near a clindamycin disk; blunting/flattening of the clindamycin zone on the side facing erythromycin (D-shaped zone) indicates inducible erm-mediated clindamycin resistance, so clindamycin should not be used. Treatment: beta-lactam or vancomycin for susceptible gram-positive cocci. Beta-lactamases: enzymatic hydrolysis of the beta-lactam ring (penicillinases, ESBLs, AmpC cephalosporinases, carbapenemases); treat by adding a beta-lactamase inhibitor, using a stable agent (carbapenem for ESBL), or switching classes for carbapenemase producers. Pseudomonas and carbapenems: (1) loss of OprD porin (chiefly imipenem), (2) upregulated efflux (MexAB-OprM, chiefly meropenem), and (3) acquired carbapenemases (metallo-beta-lactamases VIM/IMP/NDM, KPC, GES); treat per susceptibilities with an alternative active agent (e.g., ceftolozane-tazobactam or ceftazidime-avibactam for non-MBL producers).
questions.beyond_mandell: Macrolide resistance mechanisms (mef/erm) and the D test are not covered in this Pseudomonas chapter; that content rests on general antimicrobial-resistance knowledge (Mandell resistance chapters/CLSI).

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides: efflux (mefA gene, lower level resistance MIC<=16); ribosomal methylation (ermB gene, high level MIC>=64). D test checks for inducible clindamycin resistance via inducible erm gene - blunting of zone of inhibition around clindamycin proximal to erythromycin disk (D-shaped zone = positive, indicates induced clindamycin resistance); suggested treatment: beta-lactam or vancomycin for GPC, septra for MRSA. Beta-lactamases: bacteria produce enzymes breaking down beta-lactam (penicillinase, cephalosporinase/ESBL, carbapenemase); treatment depends on spectrum - use cephalosporin/aztreonam/carbapenem, add beta-lactamase inhibitor, or switch classes (tigecycline, colistin). Pseudomonas and carbapenems: porin loss (OprD deficiency confers high resistance esp to imipenem); efflux pump; carbapenemase.

Why does metronidazole not cover aerobes?

parts_raw.text: Name 2 bacteria not covered by metronidazole.
Name 2 bacteria not covered by amoxicillin.
Why does metronidazole not cover aerobes?

questions.model_answer: a) Aerobic/facultative organisms outside metronidazole's spectrum: (1) viridans streptococci (2) Actinomyces spp. b) Beta-lactamase-producing oral anaerobic gram-negative rods: (1) pigmented Prevotella spp. (2) Fusobacterium spp. (Porphyromonas spp. also acceptable). c) Metronidazole requires reductive activation by low-redox electron-transport proteins (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase/ferredoxin) found only in anaerobic bacteria; once reduced, the nitro radical fragments DNA. Aerobes lack this reductive machinery and ambient oxygen re-oxidizes any activated drug, so it is never converted to its cytotoxic form.
questions.beyond_mandell: Reductive-activation mechanism is standard pharmacology, not stated in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: a) Actinomyces; Propionibacterium acnes; Lactobacillus. b) H. flu (beta lactamase); Moraxella (beta lactamase); B. fragilis; Prevotella. c) Reductive activation only occurs in obligate anaerobes; reductive particles (nitrogen radicals) interact with DNA causing strand breakage and fatal destabilization of DNA helix.

questions.model_answer: Key distinguishing reasons for each pair: Valganciclovir over valacyclovir - CMV activity. Famciclovir over acyclovir - better oral bioavailability/less frequent dosing for HSV/VZV. Atovaquone over dapsone - G6PD deficiency (avoid dapsone hemolysis). Doxycycline over TMP-SMX - G6PD deficiency or need to avoid sulfa/renal dosing. Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate - less nephrotoxicity/infusion toxicity. Fluconazole over caspofungin - need CNS/urinary penetration or oral therapy (azole penetrates; echinocandins do not). Azithromycin over clarithromycin - fewer CYP3A4 drug interactions. Metronidazole over clindamycin - avoid C. difficile risk. Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin - better anaerobic/respiratory coverage (conversely levofloxacin for urinary/renal penetration). Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem - carbapenem-sparing to reduce resistance pressure when adequate. Ampicillin over cloxacillin - Enterococcus or Listeria coverage. Cefazolin over cloxacillin - convenient dosing/efficacy for MSSA (or penicillin allergy considerations).
